newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Former Malaysian minister faces charges in Australia.
newsitem.headline: Former Malaysian minister faces charges in Australia.

text.p: A leading Malaysian politician charged with trying to take A$1.26 million (US$930,000) in cash out of Australia without declaring it was discovered when he tried to take it aboard an aircraft as hand luggage, a Queensland court heard on Tuesday.

Former chief minister of the Malaysian state of Selangor, Muhammad Muhammad Taib appeared in the Brisbane magistrates court also charged with making a false declaration to Australian customs officials about the amount of money he was carrying.

The huge sum of cash came to light after Muhammad Taib was told at Brisbane Airport last December that his bag was too big to go with him as cabin baggage, defence lawyer Terry O'Gorman told the court at the start of the committal hearing.

"As the bag was going through the X-ray conveyor, one of the security officials said it was too big and too heavy and would have to go in the luggage compartment, and Mr Taib said 'well if this luggage has got to go in the luggage compartment I've got valuables I want to get out," O'goroan said.
Muhammad Taib, 51, was detained at Brisbane airport on December 22 1996 as he was leaving for New Zealand with money in his bags.

He resigned his Selangor post in April because of the charges but remained a vice-president of malaysia's ruling United Malays National Organisation (UMNO). The two charges Mohammad Taib faces carry maximum penalties of a A$10,000 fine and/of five years' jail.
O'Gorman said the cash, in various currencies, was to buy Mohammad Taib's three brothers three blocks of land adjoining a block he bought earlier at Sovereign Island on Queensland's Gold Coast.
Under questioning from O'Gorman, Australian Federal Police agent Glyn Lewis had claimed most of the moeny belonged to his three brothers.

Lewis also agreed that Mohammad Taib had declared on arrival in Australia on December 16 lastyear that he was carrying more than the allowable A$5,000 - although he said that he was carrying only the equivalent of less than A$10,000 in Malaysian ringgit.
Lewis also agreed that when Mohammad Taib left Australia on December 22, he was not asked to declare if he was carrying more than A$5,000.

In a police interview at Brisbane Airport, read out at Tuesday's hearing, Muhammad Taib said he wanted to invest in Australia even though many of his friends had got cold feet because of comments by race row politician Pauline Hanson, a Queensland MP.
"I love this place, I love the sea, I love the people, even though there's problem with the government," he said.
"I mean that woman (Hanson) talks about Asians and so many of my friends cancel, but no, I want to help, I want to invest, you know, and I'm getting into trouble for that.
